item.title: Beyond AI Slop: Responsible AI Use in Literature Reviews and Publishing (RCR) — Fri Oct 23, 10:00 AM — Online
item.description:
If AI can summarize hundreds of papers in seconds, what's left for you (the researcher) to do? In this RCR session, we'll examine the growing landscape of AI-generated scholarly content (including so-called "AI slop") and explore how it affects literature reviews and scholarly publication. We'll examine the limitations and biases that generative AI can introduce or amplify (e.g. hallucinations, sycophancy, and opaque provenance) and discuss practical strategies for avoiding them. We'll also discuss emerging publisher expectations regarding transparency and disclosure of AI use by authors. As AI changes what expertise looks like, attendees will learn strategies for critically assessing AI-generated outputs, recognizing potential biases, and making informed decisions about when and how AI can be used responsibly in the research process.

item.title: What to Do When Humans Are No Longer the Gold Standard — Fri Oct 23, 10:00 AM — SSRI-Gross Hall 270
item.description:
October 23, 2026 (10:00 - 11:30 am) Gross Hall 270 Arthur Spirling Class of 1987 Professor of Politics Director, Center for Statistics and Machine Learning Princeton University
What to Do When Humans Are No Longer the Gold Standard: Large Language Models, Robustness and Aggregation
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable of performing data annotation and other research tasks at, and in some cases beyond, the level of highly trained human experts. What does this mean for political science research and the conclusions we draw from it?
In this talk, Arthur Spirling will examine how increasingly capable LLMs may affect inference in downstream research. He will discuss why estimated treatment effects may become larger as models improve, while apparent null effects may become more difficult to interpret. The talk will also consider the importance of testing the sensitivity and robustness of research findings to future advances in AI, including the use of local calibration

item.title: New Frontiers in the Investigation of Online Environments and the Health of Black Americans — Fri Oct 23, 11:00 AM — None
item.description:
Online environments are ubiquitous social-ecological contexts that can change the way we think, what we believe, how we interact, and how we behave. For Black Americans, persistent mental and physical health disparities are shaped by online environments - directly and indirectly, for better and for worse, and at individual and structural levels. Existing psychological research often focuses on mental health, but the degree to which online environments catalyze health behavior change, physical health symptoms, and pre-clinical disease risk is understudied. Taking a social health psychology perspective, this talk describes emerging challenges and opportunities for investigating the physical health impacts of online environments on Black communities. A body of empirical research that draws on interdisciplinary perspectives and employs methodological plurality will be presented to make visible how online environments can shape the health of Black populations in America.
Source: Duke Unive

Keisha Bentley-Edwards and Latesha Harris examining how structural factors, including racism and socioeconomic disadvantage, interact with psychosocial stressors to shape health across the life course. The discussion will highlight emerging evidence on the biological consequences of chronic adversity, pathways to cardiometabolic risk, and the role of resilience, community strengths, and intervention science in promoting health equity.
Be part of the conversation. Join faculty, staff and students as we share new research, spark interdisciplinary exchange and build a community dedicated to advancing equity.Lunch will be provided.

item.title: CCN Colloquium: "Cognitive Convergence: Deep Similarities Between Large Language Models and Human Cognition" — Fri Oct 23, 12:00 PM — LSRC - DIBS B035 Multipurpose Room
item.description: LLMs are widely regarded as alien intelligences, systems whose cognitive operations are fundamentally unlike our own. Apparent similarities to human cognition are therefore often seen as the result of anthropomorphic projection. I argue that this framing is mistaken. LLMs clearly differ from humans in important respects, including their physical substrate, learning history, and the environments with which they interact. These differences make it all the more striking that contemporary LLM-based systems converge with human cognition on a number of principles of cognitive organization with longstanding support in cognitive science. I identify structural correspondences across five dimensions: inferential organization, computational architecture, representational structure, prediction-driven learning, and reinforcement-learning-like mechanisms supporting goal-directed control. item.title: Triangle Quantum Computing Seminar Series: Pasqal’s neutral-atom quantum computing technology — Fri Oct 23, 2:00 PM — None
item.description:
Abstract: This talk presents Pasqal's full-stack neutral-atom quantum processing unit (QPU) technology, spanning hardware architecture and the software stack. It explains how neutral-atom QPUs integrate with classical high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure to address problems that are difficult or impossible to solve using conventional computing alone. I will describe how customers use our systems today in energy, financial services, and advanced materials. The talk also highlights the company's recent technical progress, including defect-free, scalable arrays of 1,024 atoms, differential-equation benchmarks with two logical qubits, and our roadmap toward FTQC.
Bio: Heejeong Jeong is Head of Quantum Computing, US, at Pasqal US Inc. She earned a Ph.D. in Physics from Duke University in 2006, where her research included the first observation of optical precursors using cold ³⁹K atoms. item.title: Generative Statistics for the Unseen — Fri Oct 23, 3:30 PM — Old Chemistry 116
item.description:
Statistical learning is built on observed data, yet many of its most important questions concern the unseen: What could go wrong under distribution shifts? What would have happened under alternative interventions?
In this talk, I present a generative approach to these questions, using flow-based models to learn and transform probability distributions beyond observed data. I will focus on worst-case generation under Wasserstein distributional robustness, where we learn not only robust decisions but also the worst-case distributions themselves. I will discuss the underlying minimax formulation, computational algorithms, and theoretical guarantees through optimization in L2-map spaces, and then connect this framework to counterfactual inference and constrained distribution learning. Why did I name this film "Fairy Tale"? Why do we need fairy tales?
In 2020, I started editing this film. It was a special year. It seems to me to be a reboot, a reconfirmation of the present and the future.

About Holden Thorp
Holden Thorp is editor-in-chief of the “Science“ family of journals, a position he has held since 2019. He previously served as provost of Washington University in St. Louis from 2013 to 2019 and as UNC-Chapel Hill’s 10th chancellor from 2008 to 2013.
Thorp writes about science, artificial intelligence, scientific publishing and the institutions that shape research and public understanding. His recent work has examined AI’s effects on scientific research and publishing, debates over social media and teen mental health and the pressures facing universities.

item.title: Teen Science Café: Rhino Conservation — Fri Nov 6, 6:00 PM — Downtown Raleigh
item.description: One of the many tools used in conservation is translocation – moving individual animals or plants to a new area. They can be moved to establish new populations, increase existing numbers, or to remove an ongoing threat. While it can bring many benefits, translocation requires careful planning to ensure individuals thrive in their new habitat. This is especially true with endangered black rhinos, so conservation partners carefully study how animals behave, their genetic health, and source populations prior to conducting translocations. Listen to our own Dr. Liz Kierepka, as she talks about her work with the species. Teen Science Cafés bring teens together in an informal setting to learn about science and technology, on the first Friday every month during the school year. item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Wed Jan 20 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Carolina Performing Arts: Violinist Alexi Kenney and Pianist Janice Carissa — Thu Oct 22, 7:00 PM — Hill Hall
item.description:
Violinist Alexi Kenney and pianist Janice Carissa invite audiences to hear familiar works with fresh ears.
At the center of the program is The Wild Yes by composer and violinist Michi Wiancko, surrounded by music that spans geography, time, and tradition. The musical voices of composers Sibelius, Piazzolla, and inti figgis-vizueta enter the conversation, creating surprising relationships between sounds that might otherwise seem worlds apart.
Kenney and Carissa guide audiences through this remarkable musical landscape and remind us that great music is never fixed in time. Rather, it is continually revitalized by new listeners and fresh perspectives.
Student tickets always $11. Eligible for CLE. Find out more and buy tickets at: https://carolinaperformingarts.org/events/alexi-kenney-janice-carissa/
Source: UNC Chapel Hill
